unit.title: Hangul: Learning to Read Korean
unit.summary: From not knowing what 한글 is, to reading real Korean sentences aloud. Nothing here assumes any prior Korean.

gate.message: This unit must be finished before any Korean lesson unlocks. Reading has to come first — everything after this is built on it.

exercise_types.jamo_recognition: Show a letter, choose its sound (or the reverse).
exercise_types.jamo_audio: Play a sound, choose the letter that makes it.
exercise_types.syllable_decompose: Given a block, name its parts.
exercise_types.syllable_read: Read a block and choose what it says.
exercise_types.batchim_predict: Given the spelling, predict the pronunciation.
exercise_types.trace: Write the letter, stroke by stroke.

lessons.title: What is Korean, and what is 한글?
objectives: Understand that 한글 is an alphabet, not a set of pictures
Recognise that Korean letters group into square blocks
Know roughly what is coming and in what order

steps.heading: Korean is not Chinese, and 한글 is not hard
body: Korean writing is called 한글 (hangeul). It is an alphabet — 24 basic letters, each with one sound, exactly like the alphabet you already use.

It is not a set of thousands of pictures. That is Chinese characters, which are a different system. Korean occasionally borrows some (they are called 한자) but you can read newspapers, menus and messages without knowing a single one.

한글 was invented, on purpose, in 1443, by a committee working for King Sejong. Before that, Korean was written with Chinese characters that only the wealthy had time to learn. The stated goal was an alphabet an ordinary person could learn in a morning.
That goal shaped the design, and it is why you are going to move faster than you expect.

steps.heading: The one thing that looks strange at first
steps.body: English writes letters in a line: h-a-n. Korean packs the same letters into a square block: 한. Same three letters, stacked into one syllable.
steps.point: One block = one syllable. Always. So a four-block word has four syllables, and you can count them at a glance.

steps.heading: You already recognise more than you think

items.note: keo-pi. Say it out loud — that is the whole word.

steps.closing: Korean has borrowed a lot of English. Once you can read the letters, hundreds of words are free.

steps.instruction: You cannot read these yet. Just count the blocks.

points: 한글 is an alphabet with 24 basic letters.
Letters are grouped into square blocks; each block is one syllable.
It was designed to be learnable quickly, and it is.
Next: your first three vowels, and the letter that makes no sound at all.

lessons.title: Your first vowels: ㅏ ㅣ ㅗ
objectives: Understand why ㅇ is silent at the start

questions.q: One Korean block equals one what?

steps.heading: Three vowels, three shapes
steps.body: These three are drawn from just two pieces: a standing person ㅣ and the flat earth ㅡ, with a short stroke for the sun.

steps.heading: The letter that makes no sound
body: Every Korean block must start with a consonant. But 'a' has no consonant in front of it. So Korean uses a placeholder: ㅇ.
At the start of a block, ㅇ is completely silent. It is an empty chair holding the vowel's place.
아 is just 'a'. 이 is just 'i'. 오 is just 'o'. Do not try to pronounce the circle.
steps.caution: ㅇ has a second job later — underneath a block it becomes the 'ng' of 'sing'. For now: silent at the front.

steps.heading: Where the vowel sits
body: ㅏ and ㅣ stand up tall, so they go to the RIGHT of the consonant: 아, 이.
ㅗ lies flat, so it goes UNDERNEATH: 오.
That is the whole rule. Tall vowels to the right, flat vowels below.

steps.instruction: Two real Korean words, using only what you know.

points: ㅏ = a, ㅣ = i, ㅗ = o
ㅇ at the front of a block is silent
Tall vowels go right, flat vowels go below
You can now read 아이 and 오이

lessons.title: Your first consonants: ㄴ and ㅁ
objectives: Combine them with ㅏ ㅣ ㅗ

steps.heading: Two consonants you already know how to say
steps.body: ㄴ is exactly the n of 'no'. ㅁ is exactly the m of 'me'. No adjustment needed — and both letters are pictures of how your mouth makes them.

steps.heading: The letters are diagrams
body: ㄴ is a picture of your tongue tip curling up to touch the ridge behind your top teeth. Say 'n' and feel it happen.
ㅁ is a picture of your mouth, seen from the front — a closed square. Say 'm' and your lips do exactly that.
This is not a memory trick invented for learners. It is written down in the 1446 document that explains the alphabet.

points: ㄴ = n, ㅁ = m
Korean letters are drawings of the mouth
You can now read 나이 and 이모

lessons.title: The two hardest vowels: ㅓ and ㅡ
lessons.difficulty_warning: These two vowels do not exist in English. Expect to get them wrong at first — everyone does. This lesson is longer on purpose.

steps.heading: ㅓ is ㅗ with your lips relaxed
body: Say ㅗ. Feel your lips push forward into a circle.
Now make the same kind of sound but let your lips go completely slack and flat. Drop your jaw a little. That is ㅓ.
The only difference is your lips. Nothing else moves.
Use a mirror for this. If your lips move forward, you said ㅗ.

steps.heading: ㅡ is ㅜ with your lips relaxed
body: Same trick. Say ㅜ (the oo of 'food') and feel your lips round.
Now pull your lips back into a flat, wide, slightly unpleasant smile while keeping your tongue where it is. That is ㅡ.
English has nothing like ㅡ, which is why it feels odd. It is a very common vowel in Korean, so it is worth the effort now.

steps.heading: Real words that differ only in this

steps.note: Record each one. Compare against the model. This is the single best use of five minutes at this stage.

items.note: you have not met ㅠ yet — it is ㅜ with a y in front

points: ㅓ = ㅗ without rounded lips
ㅡ = ㅜ without rounded lips
These take weeks, not minutes. They will come back in every review.
You now know all ten basic vowels except the y-versions

lessons.title: ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ — the plain consonants
objectives: Understand that they sit between English g/k, d/t, b/p

steps.heading: Not quite g, not quite k
body: English splits these sounds two ways: g/k, d/t, b/p. The difference is whether your vocal cords buzz.
Korean splits them three ways, and the difference is how much AIR comes out. ㄱ ㄷ ㅂ are the quiet ones — very little air.

To an English ear they land somewhere between 'g' and 'k'. At the start of a word they sound more like k, t, p. Between two vowels they soften toward g, d, b. That is why 부산 is spelled 'Busan' but often sounds like 'Pusan'.
You do not need to control this. It happens automatically. Just do not push out a big puff of air.

points: ㄱ ㄷ ㅂ are the low-air versions
They shift between g/k, d/t, b/p depending on position — automatically
You can now read four-syllable words

lessons.title: ㅅ, ㅈ, ㅎ, ㄹ
objectives: Know that ㅅ becomes 'sh' before ㅣ

steps.heading: ㅅ has a secret
body: ㅅ is normally the s of 'sun'. But in front of an i-sound it automatically becomes 'sh'.
So 시 is 'shi', not 'si'. 사 stays 'sa'.
Nobody decides to do this — it happens in every Korean mouth. Just expect it when you see 시.

steps.heading: ㄹ is the one that takes time
body: ㄹ is not the English r and not the English l. It is one sound that lands between them.
At the start of a syllable it is a single quick flap of the tongue — the sound in the middle of American 'butter' or 'ladder'. Say 'butter' fast and notice the tongue tap. That tap is ㄹ.
At the END of a syllable it is a clear l: 물 is 'mul'.
Do not curl your tongue back like an English r. Do not hold it like an English l. Tap and move on.
This one takes weeks. That is normal, and it is not blocking anything — you can read ㄹ correctly long before you can say it perfectly.

steps.note: Tap, do not curl. Try saying 'butter' first, then 러.

points: ㅅ = s, but 'sh' before ㅣ
ㅈ = j
ㅎ = h
ㄹ = a tongue tap at the start, an l at the end. Give it time.
You now know 9 of the 14 basic consonants

lessons.title: The breathy consonants: ㅋ ㅌ ㅍ ㅊ
objectives: Hear the difference from ㄱ ㄷ ㅂ ㅈ

steps.heading: An extra stroke means more air
body: Look at these pairs: ㄱ→ㅋ, ㄷ→ㅌ, ㅂ→ㅍ, ㅈ→ㅊ. Each one has gained a stroke.
That is not decoration. In 한글, an added stroke systematically means 'the same sound, with more air'.
So you are not learning four new letters. You are learning one rule applied to four letters you already know.
Hold your palm in front of your mouth. Say ㄱ — almost nothing. Say ㅋ — you should feel a clear puff.

points: An extra stroke = more air
ㄱ→ㅋ, ㄷ→ㅌ, ㅂ→ㅍ, ㅈ→ㅊ
All 14 basic consonants are now covered

lessons.title: The tight consonants: ㄲ ㄸ ㅃ ㅆ ㅉ
lessons.difficulty_warning: This is the contrast English speakers find hardest. Recognition comes first; production takes longer, and that is fine.

steps.heading: Three, not two
body: English has two of these: 'g' and 'k'. Korean has three: ㄱ, ㅋ and ㄲ.
ㄱ = a little air. ㅋ = a lot of air. ㄲ = no air at all, with your throat squeezed tight.
To find ㄲ: imagine you are about to lift something heavy and you tense up and hold your breath. Now say 'k' from that position. Nothing should come out onto your hand.
Doubling the letter is the visual clue: ㄱㄱ written together means tighten it.

steps.note: Hold a hand in front of your mouth. ㄲ ㄸ ㅃ should move nothing at all.

points: Doubled letter = tense, no air
Korean has a three-way contrast where English has two
Recognition before production. These will keep coming back in review.
All 19 consonants are now covered

lessons.title: The y-vowels: ㅑ ㅕ ㅛ ㅠ

steps.heading: Four letters, one rule
steps.body: Add a second stroke to a vowel and you add a y in front of it. That is the entire lesson.

steps.closing: ㅡ and ㅣ have no y-versions — try saying 'y-eu' or 'y-i' and you will hear why.

points: Two strokes = add a y
All 10 basic vowels are now covered

lessons.title: Combined vowels: ㅐ ㅔ ㅘ ㅝ ㅚ ㅟ ㅢ
objectives: Know which ones have merged in modern speech

steps.heading: They sound like they look
steps.body: ㅗ + ㅏ written together is ㅘ, and it is pronounced 'wa' — ㅗ sliding into ㅏ. The compound vowels are the friendliest part of Hangul: read the parts, say them quickly, done.

steps.heading: The good news nobody tells beginners
body: ㅐ and ㅔ used to be different sounds. For most Korean speakers today they are identical. So are ㅙ, ㅚ and ㅞ.
This means you cannot learn them by ear, because there is nothing to hear. They are a spelling problem, learned word by word — exactly like 'their' and 'there' in English.
Native speakers mix them up too, and often spell 네 as 니 in messages just to keep it apart from 내.

steps.heading: ㅢ is the awkward one
body: ㅢ is pronounced three different ways depending on where it sits:
At the start of a word — a real ㅢ: 의사 (doctor).
After a consonant — simply ㅣ: 희망 is said [히망].
As the possessive particle 'of' — usually ㅔ: 우리의 is said [우리에].
One spelling, three sounds. Learn the three positions and it stops being confusing.

points: Compound vowels sound like their parts said quickly
ㅐ/ㅔ and ㅙ/ㅚ/ㅞ have merged — learn the spelling per word
ㅢ has three pronunciations depending on position
Every Korean letter is now covered. Next: the consonant that sits underneath.

lessons.title: 받침: the letter underneath
objectives: Read blocks with a final consonant

steps.heading: A little consonant sitting underneath
body: So far every block has had two parts: a consonant and a vowel. 하, 나, 가.
Sometimes a third letter sits underneath, holding the block up from below.
Korean calls it 받침 — the word literally means 'a support', the same word for the prop under a shelf.
한 is ㅎ + ㅏ + ㄴ. The ㄴ is the 받침.

steps.heading: Now the proper term
body: In linguistic terms, 받침 is the coda of the syllable — the final consonant position.
It is optional: 하 has none, 한 has one. It changes both the sound of the block and, later, which grammar particles you attach.
받침 is where nearly every Korean pronunciation rule happens. Getting comfortable with it now makes the next five lessons straightforward.

steps.heading: ㅇ finally does its other job
steps.body: Remember that ㅇ is silent at the front of a block. Underneath, it is a real sound: the ng of 'sing'. 강 is 'gang'. 사랑 is 'sarang'.

points: 받침 = the consonant underneath a block
받침 ㅇ is 'ng'; initial ㅇ is silent
받침 decides pronunciation rules AND grammar particles later

lessons.title: 27 written, 7 heard
objectives: Predict how any written 받침 is pronounced

steps.heading: Korean is strict about endings
body: 27 different letters can be written as a 받침. Only seven sounds can actually come out: ㄱ ㄴ ㄷ ㄹ ㅁ ㅂ ㅇ.
Everything else changes into whichever of the seven is closest.
So 옷 is written with ㅅ but pronounced [옫]. 꽃 is written with ㅊ but pronounced [꼳]. 부엌 is [부억].
This surprises everyone, and it is the reason spelling and pronunciation diverge in Korean.

steps.heading: Why it happens
body: At the end of a syllable, Korean stops the air and does not release it. Your tongue or lips get into position — and then just stay there.
Because nothing is released, the fine differences between ㅅ, ㅆ, ㅈ, ㅊ, ㅌ and ㅎ never get a chance to be heard. They all collapse into a held ㄷ.
Try it: say 'cat' but freeze before the t escapes. That silent, held ending is what a Korean 받침 sounds like.

generator.note: These pairs sound identical — that is the point.

points: Seven final sounds: ㄱ ㄴ ㄷ ㄹ ㅁ ㅂ ㅇ
ㅅ ㅆ ㅈ ㅊ ㅌ ㅎ all become [ㄷ] underneath
ㄲ ㅋ become [ㄱ]; ㅍ becomes [ㅂ]
Final stops are never released

lessons.title: 연음: when the 받침 moves house
objectives: Explain why 한국어 sounds like 한구거
lessons.importance: This is the single most useful pronunciation rule in Korean. Every particle and every verb ending starts with a vowel, so this fires constantly.

steps.heading: 한국어 → 한구거
body: The 받침 ㄱ in 국 is stuck underneath its block with nowhere to go.
But the very next block, 어, begins with ㅇ — which is silent. An empty chair.
So the ㄱ slides across and sits in it. 한-구-거.
Nothing is added or removed. The letters just re-shuffle across the boundary.

steps.heading: The important detail
body: When a 받침 moves, it moves as its ORIGINAL letter — not as one of the seven.
꽃 alone is [꼳]. But 꽃이 is [꼬치], not [꼬디]. The ㅊ was there all along; it just needed somewhere to go.
This is why Korean spelling keeps letters that seem never to be pronounced. They are pronounced — as soon as a vowel follows.
In linguistics this is called resyllabification. Korean calls it 연음.

steps.closing: The last one is worth saying aloud a few times. You have almost certainly heard 마시써요 without knowing why it was spelled 맛있어요.

steps.heading: Two exceptions
body: 받침 ㅇ never moves — it is already a nasal filling the slot: 강아지 stays [강아지].
받침 ㅎ vanishes instead of moving: 좋아요 is [조아요], not [조하요].

steps.instruction: Read each one aloud, applying 연음. Then check.

points: A 받침 moves into a following empty ㅇ
It moves as its original letter, not its seven-sound version
받침 ㅇ never moves; 받침 ㅎ disappears
This is why written and spoken Korean look so different

lessons.title: 경음화: why 학교 sounds like 학꾜
objectives: Apply tensification after ㄱ ㄷ ㅂ

steps.heading: Your throat is already tight
body: After a ㄱ, ㄷ or ㅂ 받침, your throat is closed and tense.
The next consonant has to start from there — so it comes out as the tight version, whether you meant it or not.
학교 becomes [학꾜]. 먹다 becomes [먹따]. 국밥 becomes [국빱].
You do not choose this. It is physically what happens.

steps.heading: The technical version
steps.body: 경음화 (tensification): a lax obstruent onset becomes tense following an obstruent coda. ㄱ→ㄲ, ㄷ→ㄸ, ㅂ→ㅃ, ㅅ→ㅆ, ㅈ→ㅉ. This one is fully automatic — no exceptions, no memorisation.

points: After ㄱ ㄷ ㅂ, the next consonant goes tense
Fully automatic, no exceptions

lessons.title: 비음화: why 감사합니다 sounds like 감사함니다

steps.heading: The mouth takes the easy route
body: In 국물, your mouth is sealed for the ㄱ, and then the ㅁ needs air out of your nose.
Rather than switch abruptly, your mouth just sends the ㄱ out of your nose too — which turns it into ㅇ. [궁물].
Same thing in 감사합니다: the ㅂ before ㄴ becomes ㅁ. [감사함니다].
You have been hearing 함니다 since your very first Korean phrase.

steps.heading: The pattern
body: Before ㄴ or ㅁ: ㄱ → [ㅇ], ㄷ → [ㄴ], ㅂ → [ㅁ].
This matters enormously because -습니다 and -ㅂ니다 are the most common formal endings in Korean, and both are affected every single time.

steps.heading: And ㄹ gets dragged in
body: After ㅁ, ㅇ, ㄱ or ㅂ, a following ㄹ turns into ㄴ. 종로 is [종노].
If the coda was ㄱ or ㅂ, that new ㄴ then triggers nasalisation as well: 국립 → 국닙 → [궁닙]. Two rules in a row.

points: Before ㄴ/ㅁ: ㄱ→ㅇ, ㄷ→ㄴ, ㅂ→ㅁ
-습니다 is always [슴니다]
ㄹ becomes ㄴ after a non-ㄹ consonant, which can then feed nasalisation

steps.heading: Squeezed in together
body: Sometimes two consonants share the space underneath one block: 값, 닭, 앉, 삶.
Korean never says both. One stays and the other goes silent.
But it is not gone forever — when a vowel comes along, the silent one wakes up and moves into it. 값 is [갑], but 값이 is [갑씨].

steps.heading: Which one survives?
body: Unfortunately this is lexical — you learn it per cluster. The good news is there are only eleven, and a handful account for almost everything you will read.
The four you will actually meet: ㄺ (닭, 읽다), ㄻ (삶, 젊다), ㄼ (여덟, 넓다), ㅄ (값, 없다).

points: Two 받침, only one sound
The silent one returns when a vowel follows
Four clusters cover most real text: ㄺ ㄻ ㄼ ㅄ

lessons.title: ㅎ: the letter that melts and vanishes

steps.heading: ㅎ is a puff of air, and air merges
body: When ㅎ meets ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ or ㅈ, the two fuse into one breathy letter: ㅋ, ㅌ, ㅍ, ㅊ.
It works in either order. 축하 → [추카] (ㄱ then ㅎ). 좋고 → [조코] (ㅎ then ㄱ).
In front of a vowel, ㅎ simply gives up and disappears. 좋아요 → [조아요].

steps.heading: What you will actually hear
body: Between a nasal and a vowel, ㅎ often weakens in ordinary speech too: 전화 becomes [저놔], 결혼 becomes [겨론], 은행 becomes [으냉].
This is not the prescriptive standard, so a textbook will tell you 전화 is [전화]. Both are worth recognising — say the standard, expect the casual.

points: ㅎ + ㄱㄷㅂㅈ → ㅋㅌㅍㅊ, in either order
ㅎ + vowel → ㅎ disappears
In casual speech ㅎ also weakens after ㄴ ㄹ ㅁ ㅇ

steps.heading: ㄴ and ㄹ cannot sit next to each other
body: They are made in nearly the same place, and switching between them mid-word is awkward. So Korean makes both of them ㄹ.
신라 → [실라]. 설날 → [설랄]. 연락 → [열락]. It works in both orders.

steps.heading: 이 pulls ㄷ and ㅌ upward
body: The 이 sound is made with your tongue high and forward. A ㄷ or ㅌ underneath gets pulled along and comes out as ㅈ or ㅊ.
같이 → [가치]. 굳이 → [구지]. 해돋이 → [해도지].
This only happens across a word boundary — inside one piece of a word nothing changes: 디자인 stays [디자인].

points: ㄴ + ㄹ or ㄹ + ㄴ → ㄹㄹ
ㄷ/ㅌ + 이 → ㅈ/ㅊ

steps.heading: Everything at once
body: Real Korean applies several rules in one word. 읽습니다 needs cluster simplification, then tensification, then nasalisation — and comes out [익씀니다].
You do not have to compute this consciously. Read the word, apply what you know, and check. The pattern-matching becomes automatic faster than you expect.

steps: the remaining ㄴ links into 아 (liaison)

steps.instruction: Read each aloud, then check your pronunciation.

steps.heading: Your first paragraph
steps.text: 안녕하세요. 저는 리티시예요. 한국어를 배워요. 한국 음식을 좋아해요. 김치찌개가 맛있어요.
steps.translation: Hello. I'm Rithish. I'm learning Korean. I like Korean food. Kimchi jjigae is delicious.
steps.note: You are not expected to understand the grammar yet. The point is that you can now READ it — every letter, every sound.

on_pass.message: 한글 마스터. You can read Korean. Everything from here on is language, not letters.

on_fail.message: Not quite yet — and that is completely normal. The letters you missed are going into your review queue and you can retake this whenever you like.

steps.heading: For the ambitious
steps.text: 한글은 1443년에 만들어졌습니다. 세종대왕이 백성들을 위해 만들었습니다.
steps.translation: Hangul was created in 1443. King Sejong made it for the common people.
steps.note: Much harder. Read it aloud without worrying about the meaning.

points: You can read every Korean letter and every syllable block
You know the seven pronunciation rules and can apply them together
Romanisation will now start fading out of your lessons — you no longer need it
Next unit: your first actual Korean sentences
